sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The northern Marche coastal zone is presently affected only by low seismic activity, but damaging earthquakes struck this area in the recent past (e.g. in 1924 and 1930, Senigallia).
The most realistic hypothesis that can be envisaged to-date on the basis of the local geologic setting considers the blind thrust-faults located at the leading-edge of the Apennine accretionary prism as the main active and probably seismogenic faults in the area. Some studies clearly dispute this information or substantially endorse it, i.e.
Coward et al. (1999) stated that thrusting and folding ended in the Early Pleistocene, and Di Bucci and Mazzoli (2002) add that NE-SW extension dominate the area today.
However, a NW-SE trending minimum stress axis and a NE-SW trending maximum compressional stress axis were shown respectively by borehole breakouts and earthquake focal mechanisms (Montone et al., 2004; Frepoli and Amato, 1997). In addition, the focal solution of the 1987 Porto San Giorgio earthquake (Mw 5.1), that occurred 50 km southeast of Ancona, indicates NE-SW horizontal compression (Pondrelli et al., 2002).
The seismogenic source of the 2 January 1924 Senigallia earthquake may be correlated with a blind thrust-fault driving the growth of the coastal anticline detected through geophysical prospecting (Bally et al., 1986) and a geomorphological study (Vannoli et al., 2004). Vannoli et al. perform a geomorphological analysis to identify the blind faults along the northern Marche coastal belt. In particular the longitudinal profiles of Metauro and Cesano rivers are warped where they cross anticline coastal axis.
Since the deformed alluvial terraces are youthful geological features, they interpret the warping processes as active. This is supported by the anomalous behaviour of the Cesano River that seems to have been forced to sweep south-eastward about 3 km from its mouth, where it also undermines the bedrock of its southern valley flank.
The geometry and width of fault at depth are based on a seismic reflection profile by Bally et al. (1986). Its length is constrained on the basis of major fluctuations of the fold axial-plane.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) What is the most reliable seismic source for the 1924 earthquake?
2) To what type of geologic structures may these sources be correlated?
3) Are the coastal anticlines presently growing?
4) May stick-slip episodes occur on this fault?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Elmi et al. (1987)
These workers analyse geometrical characteristics of alluvial terraces (convergence vs. divergence of terrace treads) and of the underlying erosion surface carved into the local bedrock to derive differential vertical movements between two areas to the north and south of the Conca river.
According to the estimated age of the alluvial terraces the northern area subsided and the southern one was uplifted during Middle-Late Pleistocene.
The two areas are separated by a tectonic line, namely "Linea del Conca", which is supposed to have been active since the Early Pliocene.
Nanni and Vivalda (1987)
They analyse the evolution of the fluvial network in the Marche region. On the basis of a geometric reconstruction of the erosion surface buried beneath the alluvial deposits and observations on the migration of river channels, these authors suggest that the fluvial network may be controlled by tectonic activity. NE oriented faults may control the drainage pattern whereas minor channel northward migrations, in the proximity of the coast, may have been driven by a growing anticline with a NE-SW trending axis. The presence of an anticline near the coastline is also revealed by the rising of the buried thalweg of rivers. Two main anticlines have been detected, the first in the area of Falconara Marittima (northern Marche); the second at Porto San Giorgio (southern Marche).
Nesci et al. (1990)
This paper analyses stratigraphic and sedimentary features of alluvial terraces of the Metauro and Foglia rivers to derive the tectonic behaviour of the Adriatic margin in the Marche region over the Middle Pleistocene -Holocene. As result the area seems to be affected by regional uplift combined with local tectonic processes. Specifically, the seaward convergence of the terrace treads is interpreted as an effect of local tilting.
Elmi et al. (1991)
They analyse geomorphic features of the alluvial terrace sequences of the Conca, Foglia, Metauro, and Esino rivers. The convergence of the terrace treads is interpreted as being the effect of significant tilting throughout the Middle Pleistocene -Holocene. The authors also question the validity of previous interpretations that link the progressive entrenchment of the river channels into the SE side of the valleys to the activity of NE-SW trending faults. The proposed explanation is that this entrenchment could be explained either as a response to differential rock erodibility or as an effect of differential exposition to solar radiation of the two valley sides. Both factors could increase the solid load of tributary streams on the NW side and in turn the development of alluvial fans that progressively make the main channel to migrate south-eastward.
Di Bucci and Mazzoli (2002)
The researchers present a review of geological and geophysical data available for the Marche coastal region, integrated with new data from the analysis of seismic reflection lines calibrated with deep well logs. In the Northern Apennines they recognize active NE -SW extension in the axial portion of the chain and the regional uplift as well. Moreover, for the external zone they propose that thrusting and related folding in this area ceased in the Early Pleistocene, in contrast with the hypothesis of active thrusting related to a subducting slab beneath the chain. This interpretation is based on the analysis of a number of reflection seismic lines, where the upper part of Quaternary deposits appears undeformed. To perform these specific considerations on Quaternary tectonics the investigators reconstruct a synthesis of Quaternary stratigraphy (1000 m thick) from well log study and detect with detail that succession on seismic reflection lines. They consider the seismicity recorded in the external sectors of the Northern Apennines (Senigallia earthquake, 1930) due to the present-day motion of the Apulia-Adria block. In the described geodynamic context the seismotectonic behaviour observed in these zones is produced by the slab detachment and the associated unbending of the foreland plate to which the regional uplift and the NE-SW compression are related.
Santini (2003)
He studies 11 new fault solutions of crustal events, with 2.9<M<4.3, using data recorded by the national seismic network of INGV in the period 1990-2000.
He analyses 9 earthquakes located in Northern Marche and calculates the fault plane solutions for these events finding that those are divided as follow: a) three solutions for pure normal-faults, b) two solutions for pure thrust faults, c) one for thrust fault with a small strike-slip, d) three solutions with unknown stress-field. Assuming that the earthquake focal mechanisms reflect the state of stress of Northern Marche, he proposes as result of his study the possibility of dividing Northern Marche region into three areas with different seismological evidences: a) the inner area of Apenninic belt, which is characterized by extension; b) the Adriatic on-shore, which shows evidence of active compression; c) the Adriatic off-shore which shows not very clear evidence of active compression.
Di Bucci et al. (2003)
These investigators integrate different kind of data to characterise the Quaternary evolution of the Metauro River basin (Northern Marche) and its facing off-shore.
They indicate the regional Pleistocene uplift as the most important evidence of active tectonics in this area and disagree with the hypothesis that uplift and its associated deformation is generated by the growth of thrust anticlines. They approach this problem putting together recently collected seismological data with geological information, such as mesostructural data, stratigraphic and geomorphic features, and integrate them with interpreted seismic lines. They analyse 83 seismic events that occurred from 1987 to 2000 and find complex results as the fault plane solutions show an ample inhomogeneity and infer that the seismological data cannot be a reliable constraint with respect to the activity or the lack of activity of the thrust front.
In addition they study distribution of the lower Metauro valley fluvial terraces and find that even fluvial morphology shows a great complexity not only related to the general uplift of the area. They conclude that the studied area presents differential movements of the substratum in a tectonic regime characterised by spatial permutation of the principal stress axes.
Vannoli et al. (2004)
These investigators focus their attention on blind and unmapped faults that could generate damaging earthquakes. To do this they study drainage and coastal system and their associated features (channel migrations/avulsions, raised/warped terraces, bedding attitude). In the Northern Marche coastal belt which is affected by historical and instrumental seismicity, they analyse anomalous drainage patterns and deformed Middle-Late Pleistocene alluvial and coastal terraces, identifying, mapping and correlating with past sea-levels, a sequence of alluvial and coastal terraces. They find out that river terraces converge downstream and that terrace treads are warped. In addition, analysing these geomorphic features, they calculate rates of the tectonic uplift at the coast line (0.1 mm/y) and at the Apennine regional divide (0.5-1.0 mm/y). The investigators suggest that local scale deformation can be due to active blind thrust faults that drive the growth of the coastal anticlines and that could be responsible for the largest earthquakes in the region, the proposed slip rate for these faults is 0.24-0.36 mm/y.
They believe that the entire thrust front from Rimini to Ancona (about 100 km)
is active and potentially seismogenic and that, since the cumulate length of faults that ruptured in known earthquakes is about 60-70 km, the "empty spaces" along the coast line may be considered as potential seismic gap.

pictures.t: Geological sketch of the Senigallia area
pictures.c: Geological sketch-map by Favali et al. [1995], showing the main rock-types and tectonic structures in the Senigallia area. Also shown is the location of a thrust front in the near offshore.

pictures.t: Main river valleys of the Marche region
pictures.c: Sketch-maps of several alluvial plains in the Marche coastal belt showing the underground drainage patterns according to Nanni and Vivalda [1987]. Notice the northward bending of the drainage direction in the lowermost reaches.

pictures.t: Thrusts and folds along the Algerian coast
pictures.c: Data from MARADJA2 and SAMRA 2005 cruises highlight the complex pattern of thrust structures thought to be active (from Kherroubi et al. [2009]).

pictures.t: Seismic reflection lines (Di Bucci and Mazzoli [2002])
pictures.c: Seismic reflection lines used by Di Bucci and Mazzoli [2002] for interpreting the present setting of the Adriatic margin of the Northern Apennines. According to these investigators, Middle-Upper Pleistocene deposits are undeformed, suggesting that thrusting and related folding ceased in the Early Pleistocene (from Di Bucci and Mazzoli [2002]).

pictures.t: Summary of thrust faults along the Adriatic coast and in the Romagna foothills
pictures.c: Representation of thrust faults along the Adriatic coast and in the Romagna Foothills by Lavecchia et al. [2003]. These investigators consider these faults active and responsible for the recent seismicity (from Lavecchia et al. [2003]).

pictures.t: Location and focal mechanism of northern Marche earthquakes
pictures.c: The distribution of the earthquake focal mechanisms in Northern Marche reflects the state of tectonic stress state of the region, characterized by three seismologically distinct areas. The coastal area shows evidence of active compression (from Santini [2003]).

pictures.t: Profiles of fluvial terraces of the central and northern Marche region
pictures.c: Profiles of fluvial terraces for six rivers in the northern Marche coastal belt. The terraces converge downstream, and are slightly warped (from Vannoli et al. [2004]).

pictures.t: Seismotectonic sketch of the 2012 seismic sequence
pictures.c: Seismotectonic sketch of the 2012 seismic sequence with geological profile. Note that the coseismic deformation of the ground-surface caused by the 2012 sequence is consistent with the characteristic of the two 2012 seismogenic sources (from Vannoli et al. [2015]).

pictures.t: Model of active tectonic tilting for the central-northern Marche region [Vannoli et al., 2004]
pictures.c: Model of active tectonics in the northern Apennines frontal prism. Notice the rates of regional tilting inferred from the convergence of fluvial terraces and the fault slip rate inferred from the warping of the terraces (from Vannoli et al. [2004]).

pictures.t: Geological sketch of the northern Marche coastal belt [Elmi et al., 1987]
pictures.c: Geological sketch-map of the northern Marche coastal belt by Elmi et al. [1987], showing several fold axes trending parallel to the coastline and the convergence loci of fluvial terrace-treads.
